claim: Insects detect volatile molecules using olfactory (OR) or ionotropic receptors (IR) and in some cases gustatory receptors (GRs).
source: Insects detect volatile molecules using olfactory (OR) or ionotropic receptors (IR) and in some cases gustatory receptors (GRs).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about insect chemoreception systems.

claim: IRs are expressed in olfactory organs across Protostomia.
source: While IRs are expressed in olfactory organs across Protostomia, ORs have been hypothesized to be an adaptation to a terrestrial insect lifestyle.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior research on IR distribution.

claim: ORs have been hypothesized to be an adaptation to a terrestrial insect lifestyle.
source: While IRs are expressed in olfactory organs across Protostomia, ORs have been hypothesized to be an adaptation to a terrestrial insect lifestyle.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature that the authors are testing.

claim: ORs and Orco are with very high probability lacking in Lepismachilis.
source: ORs and the olfactory coreceptor (Orco) are with very high probability lacking in Lepismachilis
evidence: This is a primary finding based on transcriptome analysis and multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: Three Orco candidates were identified in Thermobia.
source: in Thermobia we have identified three Orco candidates
evidence: This is a primary finding based on transcriptome sequencing and molecular analysis.

claim: Phyllium has a fully developed OR/Orco-based system.
source: in Phyllium a fully developed OR/Orco-based system.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on transcriptome analysis showing both ORs and Orco.

claim: ORs did not arise as an adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle.
source: We suggest that ORs did not arise as an adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle, but evolved later in insect evolution, with Orco being present before the appearance of ORs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the comparative data across the three species studied.

claim: ORs evolved later in insect evolution.
source: We suggest that ORs did not arise as an adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle, but evolved later in insect evolution, with Orco being present before the appearance of ORs.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of ORs and Orco across the studied species.

claim: Orco was present before the appearance of ORs.
source: We suggest that ORs did not arise as an adaptation to a terrestrial lifestyle, but evolved later in insect evolution, with Orco being present before the appearance of ORs.
evidence: This is inferred from finding Orco candidates in Thermobia without conventional ORs, while both are absent in Lepismachilis.

claim: The molecular identity of olfactory receptors was first unraveled in vertebrates.
source: The molecular identity of olfactory receptors was first unraveled in vertebrates (Buck and Axel, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buck and Axel 1991.

claim: In mammals, as many as 1000 heterotrimeric GTP-binding protein (or G protein)-coupled receptors are considered to be employed in olfactory discrimination.
source: In mammals, as many as 1000 heterotrimeric GTP-binding protein (or G protein)-coupled receptors are considered to be employed in olfactory discrimination (Buck and Axel, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buck and Axel 1991.

claim: About 1300 receptor genes and 400 pseudogenes have been hypothesized for Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: A similar number of chemoreceptors, with about 1300 receptor genes and 400 pseudogenes, have been hypothesized for Caenorhabditis elegans (Robertson and Thomas, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robertson and Thomas 2006.

claim: All data on insect olfactory receptors are based on studies investigating the neopteran insects.
source: All data on insect olfactory receptors are based on studies investigating the neopteran insects (overview of insect order relationship is given in Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: The identity of receptors involved in olfaction in the evolutionarily more ancient apterygote insects (Archaeognatha, Zygentoma) and paleopteran insects (Odonata and Ephemeroptera) is completely unknown.
source: The identity of receptors involved in olfaction in the evolutionarily more ancient apterygote insects (Archaeognatha, Zygentoma) and paleopteran insects (Odonata and Ephemeroptera) is thus completely unknown.
evidence: This describes the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: In neopteran insects most volatile stimuli are recognized by members of the olfactory receptor family (ORs).
source: In neopteran insects (Polyneoptera, Paraneoptera, and Holometabola) most volatile stimuli are recognized by members of the olfactory receptor family (ORs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neopteran insect olfaction.

claim: ORs are multitransmembrane domain proteins unrelated to nematode or vertebrate olfactory receptors.
source: ORs are multitransmembrane domain proteins unrelated to nematode or vertebrate olfactory receptors (Mombaerts, 1999; Robertson, 2001; Hill et al., 2002), displaying a distinct membrane topology (Benton et al., 2006; Lundin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ORs display a distinct membrane topology.
source: ORs are multitransmembrane domain proteins unrelated to nematode or vertebrate olfactory receptors (Mombaerts, 1999; Robertson, 2001; Hill et al., 2002), displaying a distinct membrane topology (Benton et al., 2006; Lundin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benton et al., 2006 and Lundin et al., 2007.

claim: The number of functional OR genes varies from 10 in the human body louse Pediculus humanus humanus to about 60 in Drosophila melanogaster and up to 350 OR genes in ants.
source: The number of functional OR genes varies from 10 in the human body louse Pediculus humanus humanus (Kirkness et al., 2010) to about 60 in Drosophila melanogaster (Clyne et al., 1999; Gao and Chess, 1999; Vosshall et al., 1999) and up to 350 OR genes in ants (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting OR gene numbers in different species.

claim: ORs have been suggested to be distantly related to the gustatory receptors of arthropods.
source: ORs have been suggested to be distantly related to the gustatory receptors of arthropods, with some proteins containing a signature motif in the carboxyl terminus (Scott et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scott et al., 2001.

claim: Insect olfactory receptors function as heteromultimers composed of at least one ligand-specific OR and the coreceptor Orco.
source: Insect olfactory receptors function as heteromultimers composed of at least one ligand-specific OR and the coreceptor Orco (Vosshall et al., 1999; Elmore et al., 2003; Krieger et al., 2003; Larsson et al., 2004; Sato et al., 2008; Wicher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Orco is highly conserved among insects.
source: Interestingly, while Orco (Vosshall and Hansson, 2011) is highly conserved among insects, the sequences of other olfactory receptor genes exhibit very little sequence similarity even within the same insect order (Krieger et al., 2003), complicating their identification.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The sequences of other olfactory receptor genes exhibit very little sequence similarity even within the same insect order.
source: Interestingly, while Orco (Vosshall and Hansson, 2011) is highly conserved among insects, the sequences of other olfactory receptor genes exhibit very little sequence similarity even within the same insect order (Krieger et al., 2003), complicating their identification.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krieger et al., 2003.

claim: Orco homologues have been identified in Lepidoptera, Diptera, Coleoptera, Hymenoptera, Hemiptera, and Orthoptera.
source: So far, Orco homologues have been identified in Lepidoptera, Diptera, Coleoptera, Hymenoptera, Hemiptera (Krieger et al., 2003; Pitts et al., 2004; Smadja et al., 2009), and Orthoptera (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neither Orco nor ORs are present in the genome of the crustacean Daphnia pulex.
source: Neither Orco nor ORs are present in the genome of the crustacean Daphnia pulex, indicating that ORs are insect specific.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of Daphnia pulex.

claim: ORs are insect specific.
source: Neither Orco nor ORs are present in the genome of the crustacean Daphnia pulex, indicating that ORs are insect specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of ORs in Daphnia pulex genome.

claim: GRs were found in Crustacea, just as in insects.
source: However, GRs were found in Crustacea, just as in insects (Peñalva-Arana et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peñalva-Arana et al., 2009.

claim: IRs are involved in insect chemosensation.
source: A second receptor family, the variant ionotropic glutamate receptors (IRs), is also involved in insect chemosensation (Benton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benton et al., 2009.

claim: IRs act in combinations of up to three subunits; individual odor-specific receptors and one or two of the broadly expressed coreceptors IR25a, IR8a, and IR76b.
source: IRs act in combinations of up to three subunits; individual odor-specific receptors and one or two of the broadly expressed coreceptors IR25a, IR8a, and IR76b (Abuin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abuin et al., 2011.

claim: Two conserved members of the IR group were described in the Daphnia genome.
source: IRs are present in olfactory tissues across the Protostomia (Croset et al., 2010), for example two conserved members of this group were described in the Daphnia genome (Croset et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: The coreceptor IR25a homologue is expressed in many, if not all mature OSNs of the American lobster Homarus americanus.
source: the coreceptor IR25a homologue is expressed in many, if not all mature OSNs of the American lobster Homarus americanus (Hollins et al., 2003) and the spiny lobster Panulirus argus (Tadesse et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hollins et al., 2003.

claim: The coreceptor IR25a homologue is expressed in the spiny lobster Panulirus argus.
source: the coreceptor IR25a homologue is expressed in many, if not all mature OSNs of the American lobster Homarus americanus (Hollins et al., 2003) and the spiny lobster Panulirus argus (Tadesse et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tadesse et al., 2011.

claim: Crustaceans are the closest relatives of insects.
source: Since crustaceans are the closest relatives of insects (Friedrich and Tautz, 1995; Boore et al., 1998; Regier et al., 2010), IRs are most likely the ancient type of insect olfactory receptor.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: IRs are most likely the ancient type of insect olfactory receptor.
source: Since crustaceans are the closest relatives of insects (Friedrich and Tautz, 1995; Boore et al., 1998; Regier et al., 2010), IRs are most likely the ancient type of insect olfactory receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of IRs in crustaceans and their phylogenetic relationship to insects.

claim: Hexapods derived from an aquatic crustacean ancestor, probably in the Early Ordovician, approximately 483 mya.
source: Hexapods derived from an aquatic crustacean ancestor, probably in the Early Ordovician, approximately 483 mya (Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rota-Stabelli et al., 2013.

claim: One proposed hypothesis has been that Orco and ORs of the insect type are an adaptation to terrestrial lifestyle.
source: One proposed hypothesis has been that Orco and ORs of the insect type are an adaptation to this terrestrial lifestyle (Robertson et al., 2003; Krång et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: On the antennae of L. y-signata the only putative olfactory sensilla were porous olfactory basiconic sensilla.
source: On the antennae of L. y-signata the only putative olfactory sensilla were porous olfactory basiconic sensilla (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is based on SEM morphological analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Porous olfactory basiconic sensilla in L. y-signata were arranged in a pattern that is highly stereotypical between antennal modules composed of 5–12 annuli.
source: These sensilla were arranged in a pattern that is highly stereotypical between antennal modules composed of 5–12 annuli, with annuli typically containing zero-to-four Sensilla basiconica (Missbach et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations and supported by citation to Missbach et al., 2011.

claim: Responses to all tested chemical classes of odors, including acids, alcohols, aldehydes, esters, and ketones, were recorded from OSNs housed in basiconic sensilla of L. y-signata.
source: Responses to all tested chemical classes of odors, including acids, alcohols, aldehydes, esters, and ketones, were recorded from OSNs housed in these sensilla using the single sensillum recoding measurements (SSR) (Figure 3, uppermost heat map).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: 12 OSN types were identified in L. y-signata, present in five functional basiconic sensillum types.
source: Based on the response profile, spontaneous activity, and colocalization inside the same sensillum, we identified 12 OSN types, present in five functional basiconic sensillum types.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological characterization.

claim: Out of the 12 OSN types in L. y-signata, only seven responded to odors tested.
source: Out of the 12 OSN types, only seven responded to odors tested; two exclusively to acids, while five responded with a similar activity rate to acids or amines and to other odors.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data.

claim: Two OSN types in L. y-signata responded exclusively to acids.
source: Out of the 12 OSN types, only seven responded to odors tested; two exclusively to acids, while five responded with a similar activity rate to acids or amines and to other odors.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data.

claim: Five OSN types in L. y-signata responded with a similar activity rate to acids or amines and to other odors.
source: Out of the 12 OSN types, only seven responded to odors tested; two exclusively to acids, while five responded with a similar activity rate to acids or amines and to other odors.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data.

claim: OSNs belonging to the second class in L. y-signata were broadly tuned and exhibited relatively low spiking activity.
source: OSNs belonging to this second class were broadly tuned and exhibited relatively low spiking activity.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological characterization.

claim: OSN classes in L. y-signata displayed a low baseline activity with about 1 to 7 spikes/s, with Lys-ab2A that had a spontaneous activity of more than 25 spikes/s as the only exception.
source: In general, OSN classes displayed a low baseline activity with about 1 to 7 spikes/s, with Lys-ab2A that had a spontaneous activity of more than 25 spikes/s as the only exception.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Only rarely was an increase in spiking rate of more than 60 spikes per second recorded in L. y-signata, even for the best identified ligands.
source: Only rarely was an increase in spiking rate of more than 60 spikes per second recorded, even for the best identified ligands (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data.

claim: No responses were obtained for ammonia or pyridine in L. y-signata.
source: No responses were obtained for ammonia or pyridine.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological testing.

claim: Coeloconic-like sensilla, s-shaped trichoid sensilla, and chaetic sensilla in L. y-signata did not display any morphological features indicating olfactory function and did not respond to any odor tested.
source: Coeloconic-like sensilla, s-shaped trichoid sensilla, and chaetic sensilla did not display any morphological features indicating olfactory function and did also not respond to any odor tested (Missbach et al., 2011; data not shown).
evidence: This is based on morphological and electrophysiological analysis.

claim: 7 OSN types in L. y-signata that were all housed in basiconic sensilla responded to a wide spectrum of odor molecules.
source: In conclusion, 7 OSN types that were all housed in basiconic sensilla responded to a wide spectrum of odor molecules.
evidence: This is a summary of the electrophysiological findings.

claim: The morphology of the zygentoman antenna and its sensilla was similar to that of L. y-signata, with the presence of grooved sensilla as the only exception.
source: The morphology of the zygentoman antenna and its sensilla was similar to that of L. y-signata, with the presence of grooved sensilla as the only exception (Figure 2G; Adel, 1984; Berg and Schmidt, 1997).
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations.

claim: Five different functional types of olfactory sensilla were present in T. domestica.
source: Five different functional types of olfactory sensilla were present (Figure 3: three porous, two grooved s. basiconica, the latter are indicated by blue caption).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological characterization shown in Figure 3.

claim: In T. domestica, a nascent functional and spatial separation of the detection of amines and acids, and ketones and alcohols appeared.
source: In contrast to L. y-signata, a nascent functional and spatial separation of the detection of amines and acids, and ketones and alcohols appeared in T. domestica.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data comparing response patterns.

claim: In T. domestica, amines and acids primarily elicited responses in OSNs of grooved sensilla.
source: The former primarily elicited responses in OSNs of grooved sensilla, while less polar ones were mainly detected by porous sensilla.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from different sensillum types.

claim: In T. domestica, less polar odors were mainly detected by porous sensilla.
source: The former primarily elicited responses in OSNs of grooved sensilla, while less polar ones were mainly detected by porous sensilla.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from different sensillum types.

claim: Most of the OSNs in porous sensilla of T. domestica exhibited broad tuning and responded to at least one of the tested acids or amines as well.
source: However, most of the OSNs in porous sensilla exhibited broad tuning and responded to at least one of the tested acids or amines as well.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological characterization.

claim: The leaf insect P. siccifolium displayed a strong sexual antennal dimorphism, with males having very long antennae covered with trichoid sensilla, and the females very short antennae without trichoid sensilla.
source: Unlike the other analyzed species, the leaf insect P. siccifolium displayed a strong sexual antennal dimorphism, with males having very long antennae covered with trichoid sensilla (Figure 2L), and the females very short antennae without trichoid sensilla (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The response repertoire of P. siccifolium was much more diverse than the wingless insects, with a total of 23 different functional sensillum types identified by SSR recordings.
source: In comparison to the wingless insects, the response repertoire of the leaf insect was much more diverse, with a total of 23 different functional sensillum types as identified by SSR recordings (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: No responses were obtained from trichoid sensilla in P. siccifolium.
source: No responses were obtained from trichoid sensilla, but since they were only present on the male antennae they could be involved in detection of an unknown volatile pheromone.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological testing.

claim: Trichoid sensilla in P. siccifolium could be involved in detection of an unknown volatile pheromone.
source: No responses were obtained from trichoid sensilla, but since they were only present on the male antennae they could be involved in detection of an unknown volatile pheromone.
evidence: This is speculation based on the male-specific presence of these sensilla and lack of response to tested odors.

claim: Reported detection of volatile pheromones in insects is dependent on very specific ORs.
source: In all cases, reported detection of volatile pheromones in insects is dependent on very specific ORs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pheromone detection in insects.

claim: Leaf insects have a much broader response repertoire with a higher number of different OSN types than the more basal species analyzed.
source: Taken together these data suggest that leaf insects have a much broader response repertoire with a higher number of different OSN types than the more basal species we analyzed
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative electrophysiological data.

claim: The number of olfactory receptors has increased in leaf insects.
source: Taken together these data suggest that leaf insects have a much broader response repertoire with a higher number of different OSN types than the more basal species we analyzed; apparently the number of olfactory receptors has increased.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased diversity of functional sensillum types.

claim: At least the leaf insect makes use of ORs in odorant detection.
source: It also seems likely that at least the leaf insect makes use of ORs in odorant detection.
evidence: This is inferred from the broader response repertoire and later confirmed by transcriptome data.

claim: 99'504'815 reads were generated for the two L. y-signata chemosensory transcriptomes, out of which 77'060'687 were paired end reads.
source: In total 99'504'815 reads were generated for the two L. y-signata chemosensory transcriptomes, out of which 77'060'687 were paired end reads.
evidence: This is technical data about the sequencing effort.

claim: 25'242'666 reads were generated for pooled RNA of whole bodies and heads of L. y-signata.
source: In addition to the transcriptomes of chemosensory tissues, we sequenced pooled RNA of whole bodies and heads resulting in 25'242'666 reads.
evidence: This is technical data about the sequencing effort.

claim: 27'704'231 reads were generated for antennae of T. domestica.
source: 27'704'231 and 30'762'777 reads were generated for antennae of T. domestica and P. siccifolium, respectively
evidence: This is technical data about the sequencing effort.

claim: 30'762'777 reads were generated for antennae of P. siccifolium.
source: 27'704'231 and 30'762'777 reads were generated for antennae of T. domestica and P. siccifolium, respectively
evidence: This is technical data about the sequencing effort.

claim: Neither OR- nor Orco-coding transcripts were identified in the transcriptomes of L. y-signata using BLAST and HMM domain profile searches.
source: Neither OR- nor Orco-coding transcripts were identified in the transcriptomes of L. y-signata using BLAST and HMM domain profile searches as described in the 'Material and methods' section.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Custom HMMR-profiles directed against conserved regions of Orco proteins failed to identify any Orco-related sequences in the bristletail transcriptome.
source: Custom HMMR-profiles directed against conserved regions of Orco proteins also failed to identify any Orco-related sequences in the bristletail transcriptome.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Five GR candidates were discovered in L. y-signata.
source: We discovered five GR candidates.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: MSA analysis of L. y-signata GR candidates together with ORs and GRs of various insect species and the Daphnia GRs always confirmed the position of the L. y-signata GR candidates within the GR and not the OR family.
source: MSA analysis of these together with ORs and GRs of various insect species and the Daphnia GRs always confirmed the position of the L. y-signata GR candidates within the GR and not the OR family (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 4—source data 2, Figure 4—source data 3, Figure 4—source data 4, Figure 4—source data 5).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression levels of gustatory receptors are very low even in gustatory tissue.
source: Since expression levels of gustatory receptors are very low even in gustatory tissue (Clyne et al., 2000; Scott et al., 2001), we argue that ORs or at least Orco should be represented in the large, sensory tissue-specific transcriptome data set of L. y-signata if they are indeed part of the olfactory system in the species.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clyne et al., 2000 and Scott et al., 2001.

claim: ORs or at least Orco should be represented in the large, sensory tissue-specific transcriptome data set of L. y-signata if they are indeed part of the olfactory system in the species.
source: Since expression levels of gustatory receptors are very low even in gustatory tissue (Clyne et al., 2000; Scott et al., 2001), we argue that ORs or at least Orco should be represented in the large, sensory tissue-specific transcriptome data set of L. y-signata if they are indeed part of the olfactory system in the species.
evidence: This is a logical argument based on the depth of sequencing and known expression patterns.

claim: Three different Orco-related sequences were identified in the transcriptome of T. domestica.
source: In contrast to L. y-signata, three different Orco-related sequences were identified in the transcriptome of T. domestica.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: All three T. domestica Orco candidates were cloned as full-length coding sequences using RACE-PCR.
source: All candidates were cloned as full-length coding sequences using RACE-PCR.
evidence: This describes the molecular validation method used.

claim: The three T. domestica Orco sequences displayed different similarities to the Orco sequence of D. melanogaster: one sequence shared 45.8%, one 35.1%, and the third 24.4% sequence similarity at the amino acid level.
source: The three sequences displayed different similarities to the Orco sequence of D. melanogaster, one sequence shared 45.8%, one 35.1%, and the third 24.4% sequence similarity at the amino acid level.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Orco was the protein most similar to all three T. domestica Orco candidate sequences.
source: Orco was the protein most similar to all three Orco candidate sequences (Figures 4B and 5)
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity analysis shown in Figures 4B and 5.

claim: Some of the key amino acids of the coreceptor are substituted at least in TdomOrco3.
source: although some of the key amino acids of the coreceptor are substituted at least in TdomOrco3 (Wicher et al., 2008; Sargsyan et al., 2011; Nakagawa et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2013; highlighted in alignment Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5 and supported by citations.

claim: Apart from the Orco variants, no OR-related sequences were identified in T. domestica.
source: Apart from the Orco variants, no OR-related sequences were identified
evidence: This is a primary finding based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: 9 contigs for GR candidates were found in T. domestica that were assigned to seven GRs.
source: but 9 contigs for GR candidates were found that were assigned to seven GRs, including three candidates close to full length or full length and four additional fragments (Table 2 and Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: In the transcriptome data set of P. siccifolium, both various OR-related sequences and a single Orco sequence were detected.
source: In the transcriptome data set of P. siccifolium, both various OR-related sequences and a single Orco sequence were detected (Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: In total, 30 gene fragments coding ORs were identified in P. siccifolium.
source: However, in total, we identified 30 gene fragments coding ORs, indicating that the transcriptomic approach chosen was applicable to our question, successfully identifying both Orco and ORs in P. siccifolium.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: The transcriptomic approach successfully identified both Orco and ORs in P. siccifolium.
source: However, in total, we identified 30 gene fragments coding ORs, indicating that the transcriptomic approach chosen was applicable to our question, successfully identifying both Orco and ORs in P. siccifolium.
evidence: This validates the methodology by showing it can detect ORs when present.

claim: For all other insects analyzed so far one Orco is the norm.
source: Considering that for all other insects analyzed so far one Orco is the norm, the appearance of three Orco candidates in T. domestica is highly unusual.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: The appearance of three Orco candidates in T. domestica is highly unusual.
source: Considering that for all other insects analyzed so far one Orco is the norm, the appearance of three Orco candidates in T. domestica is highly unusual.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other insects.

claim: For all three T. domestica Orco types expression was limited to the antenna.
source: For all three Orco types expression was limited to the antenna (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In situ hybridization with an antisense probe of TdomOrco1 led to staining of single cells below one or two basiconic sensilla of an antennal subsegment.
source: To further assess the expression, we used in situ hybridization employing an antisense probe of one of the coreceptors. This led to staining of single cells below one or two basiconic sensilla of an antennal subsegment (Figure 7)
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 7.

claim: TdomOrco1 might be expressed in OSNs.
source: This led to staining of single cells below one or two basiconic sensilla of an antennal subsegment (Figure 7), suggesting that TdomOrco1 might indeed be expressed in OSNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH localization pattern.

claim: Only one neuron per sensillum was stained with TdomOrco1 probe.
source: However, only one neuron per sensillum was stained.
evidence: This is based on FISH observations.

claim: No signals were obtained when using a sense probe for TdomOrco1.
source: No signals were obtained when using a sense probe for TdomOrco1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a negative control for the FISH experiment.

claim: A high number of putative glutamate receptor coding contigs was identified in the bristletail transcriptome.
source: As none of the experiments gave a hint for the existence of any OR or Orco-related sequence in the bristletail transcriptome, we focused on the second olfactory receptor family of insects, the IRs. Although we could not identify any OR sequences in the transcriptome, a high number of putative glutamate receptor coding contigs was identified (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: Only five candidate iGluRs and 14 candidate IRs appeared to be real unigenes in L. y-signata, possessing at least two of the three transmembrane domains.
source: However, only five candidate iGluRs and 14 candidate IRs appeared to be real unigenes, possessing at least two of the three transmembrane domains.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the transcriptome data.

claim: Some candidate IR sequences were extended in 3'-direction using RACE-PCR with antennal cDNA as template, allowing verification of unigene status and antennal expression.
source: Some candidate sequences were extended in 3'-direction using RACE-PCR with antennal cDNA as template, allowing verification of unigene status and antennal expression.
evidence: This describes the molecular validation approach.

claim: The identified IRs in L. y-signata grouped with DmelIRs in MSA and phylogenetic analysis.
source: In MSA and phylogenetic analysis, the identified IRs grouped with DmelIRs (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Among the identified putative LsigIRs were orthologues of the D. melanogaster coreceptors IR25a and IR8a, as well as one receptor similar to IR76b.
source: Among the identified putative LsigIRs were orthologues of the D. melanogaster coreceptors IR25a and IR8a, as well as one receptor similar to IR76b (Figure 8A, Figure 8—source data 1, Figure 8—source data 2, Figure 8—source data 3, Figure 8—source data 4, Figure 8—source data 5).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: One or several key amino acids in the predicted glutamate binding domains were absent in the non-coreceptor IR candidates and LsigIR76b.
source: As in other IRs (Benton et al., 2009) one or several key amino acids in the predicted glutamate binding domains were absent in the non-coreceptor IR candidates and LsigIR76b (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 8B and supported by citation.

claim: 7 out of 14 LsigIRs group close to a cluster of D. pulex IRs and the antennal IRs IR21a and IR68a of D. melanogaster, with no clear relationship to one or the other.
source: 7 out of 14 LsigIRs group close to a cluster of D. pulex IRs and the antennal IRs IR21a and IR68a of D. melanogaster, with no clear relationship to one or the other.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: None of the Lepismachilis IR candidates grouped with the 'divergent' Drosophila IRs.
source: None of the Lepismachilis IR candidates grouped with the 'divergent' Drosophila IRs.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Antisense probes of IR25a and IR8a led to labeling of one to three OSNs underneath basiconic sensilla in L. y-signata.
source: Antisense probes of IR25a and IR8a led to labeling of one to three OSNs underneath basiconic sensilla (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on FISH data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: In control experiments with sense probes, or without any probe, no staining was obtained in L. y-signata.
source: In control experiments with sense probes, or without any probe, no staining was obtained (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a negative control for the FISH experiments.

claim: The pattern of expression of IR coreceptors in OSNs of L. y-signata indicates that most OSNs are covered by this gene family.
source: The pattern of expression of IR coreceptors in OSNs of L. y-signata indicates that most OSNs are covered by this gene family.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH expression pattern.

claim: The olfactory system of L. y-signata is not based on ORs.
source: Based on these results we propose that the olfactory system of L. y-signata is not based on ORs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on the absence of ORs/Orco and presence of IRs.

claim: In D. melanogaster IRs are the functional receptor type of OSNs in double-walled coeloconic sensilla.
source: In D. melanogaster IRs are the functional receptor type of OSNs in double-walled coeloconic sensilla, and ORs are predominantly expressed in OSNs housed in single-walled basiconic and trichoid sensilla (Hallem et al., 2004; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hallem et al., 2004 and Silbering et al., 2011.

claim: In D. melanogaster ORs are predominantly expressed in OSNs housed in single-walled basiconic and trichoid sensilla.
source: In D. melanogaster IRs are the functional receptor type of OSNs in double-walled coeloconic sensilla, and ORs are predominantly expressed in OSNs housed in single-walled basiconic and trichoid sensilla (Hallem et al., 2004; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hallem et al., 2004 and Silbering et al., 2011.

claim: The organization of IRs in coeloconic sensilla and ORs in basiconic/trichoid sensilla cannot exist with just one sensillum type present.
source: It follows that this organization cannot exist with just one sensillum type present, as is the case in Archaeognatha (Berg and Schmidt, 1997; Missbach et al., 2011) and older hexapod taxa as the Collembola (Altner and Prillinger, 1980).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on morphological constraints.

claim: The oldest insect taxon where double-walled sensilla were investigated is Zygentoma.
source: The oldest insect taxon where double-walled sensilla were investigated is Zygentoma, which have both single-walled basiconic sensilla with pores and double-walled sensilla with spoke channels (Berg and Schmidt, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berg and Schmidt, 1997.

claim: Zygentoma have both single-walled basiconic sensilla with pores and double-walled sensilla with spoke channels.
source: The oldest insect taxon where double-walled sensilla were investigated is Zygentoma, which have both single-walled basiconic sensilla with pores and double-walled sensilla with spoke channels (Berg and Schmidt, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berg and Schmidt, 1997.

claim: The coeloconic structure has been thought to be a prerequisite for IR function.
source: The coeloconic structure has been thought to be a prerequisite for IR function (Benton et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benton et al., 2009 and Guo et al., 2014.

claim: In the Archaeognatha IRs are most likely located in OSNs of Sensilla basiconica.
source: However, in the Archaeognatha we find that IRs are most likely located in OSNs of Sensilla basiconica.
evidence: This is based on the FISH localization data in L. y-signata.

claim: IRs might have evolved in a single-walled sensillum and did not find their modern, coeloconic environment until neopteran insects evolved.
source: IRs might thus have evolved in a single-walled sensillum and did not find their modern, coeloconic environment until neopteran insects evolved.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in Archaeognatha.

claim: Many of the OSNs in L. y-signata are very broadly tuned, responding to volatiles with several different functional groups at higher doses.
source: In the bristletail L. y-signata, we found that many of the OSNs are very broadly tuned, responding to volatiles with several different functional groups at higher doses.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data.

claim: Broadly tuned receptors might not have high affinities.
source: However, broadly tuned receptors might not have high affinities.
evidence: This is speculation about receptor properties.

claim: By counting and integrating molecules over longer times, OSNs could include even low-probability binding events in generating their response.
source: By counting and integrating molecules over longer times, OSNs could include even low-probability binding events in generating their response (Firestein, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Firestein, 2001.

claim: The system might not have a high temporal resolution, which seems to be a fair trade-off for a walking insect that lives in its substrate.
source: This might also mean that the system does not have a high temporal resolution, which seems to be a fair trade-off for a walking insect that lives in its substrate.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications.

claim: The response spectrum of Drosophila IRs is much narrower than the responses found in the bristletail.
source: The response spectrum of Drosophila IRs is much narrower than the responses we find in the bristletail.
evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological data.

claim: If IRs are the only olfactory receptor type in basal insects they should exhibit a broader spectrum of possible ligands.
source: If IRs are the only olfactory receptor type in basal insects they should exhibit a broader spectrum of possible ligands, including acids, aldehydes, alcohols, but also esters and ketones, as revealed in our physiological measurements.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the physiological data.

claim: One hypothesis to explain an IR-based olfactory system in L. y-signata would be very broad tuning of single receptors.
source: One hypothesis to explain an IR-based olfactory system in L. y-signata would be very broad tuning of single receptors, another that the selectivity of OSNs could be regulated by combinations of different IRs.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The selectivity of OSNs could be regulated by combinations of different IRs.
source: One hypothesis to explain an IR-based olfactory system in L. y-signata would be very broad tuning of single receptors, another that the selectivity of OSNs could be regulated by combinations of different IRs.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: In D. melanogaster, one conserved IR (IR64a) is expressed in different subpopulations of sensilla in the third chamber of the sacculus.
source: In D. melanogaster, one conserved IR (IR64a) is expressed in different subpopulations of sensilla in the third chamber of the sacculus (Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silbering et al., 2011.

claim: Corresponding OSNs expressing IR64a are activated either by free protons or organic acids and many other odors, including esters, alcohols, and ketones.
source: Corresponding OSNs are activated either by free protons or organic acids and many other odors, including esters, alcohols, and ketones (Ai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ai et al., 2010.

claim: Expression of IR64a together with IR8a is both necessary and sufficient for sensitivity towards organic acids and other odors.
source: Expression of this IR together with IR8a is both necessary and sufficient for sensitivity towards organic acids and other odors, but probably requires a different, until now unknown cofactor to mediate the specific response of OSNs to inorganic acids and CO2 (Ai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ai et al., 2010.

claim: IR64a/IR8a probably requires a different, until now unknown cofactor to mediate the specific response of OSNs to inorganic acids and CO2.
source: Expression of this IR together with IR8a is both necessary and sufficient for sensitivity towards organic acids and other odors, but probably requires a different, until now unknown cofactor to mediate the specific response of OSNs to inorganic acids and CO2 (Ai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ai et al., 2010.

claim: GR candidates could account for part of the non-neopteran olfactory setup.
source: Alternatively, GR candidates could account for part of the non-neopteran olfactory setup, especially since it has been shown that GRs can add to the olfactory repertoire (Tauxe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Tauxe et al., 2013.

claim: GRs can add to the olfactory repertoire.
source: Alternatively, GR candidates could account for part of the non-neopteran olfactory setup, especially since it has been shown that GRs can add to the olfactory repertoire (Tauxe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tauxe et al., 2013.

claim: Putative contact chemosensory sensilla are highly abundant on the antennae of L. y-signata and T. domestica.
source: Putative contact chemosensory sensilla are highly abundant on the antennae of L. y-signata (Missbach et al., 2011) and T. domestica (Adel, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Detection of sugars/amino acids in T. domestica likely involves GRs.
source: Both detection of sugars/amino acids (shown for T. domestica: Hansen-Delkeskamp, 2001) and a proposed contact-pheromone (Fröhlich and Lu, 2013) likely involve GRs
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: A proposed contact-pheromone likely involves GRs.
source: Both detection of sugars/amino acids (shown for T. domestica: Hansen-Delkeskamp, 2001) and a proposed contact-pheromone (Fröhlich and Lu, 2013) likely involve GRs
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fröhlich and Lu, 2013.

claim: Involvement of the limited set of GRs beyond contact chemosensation is unlikely.
source: indicating that involvement of the limited set of GRs beyond this scope is unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of GRs.

claim: So far only one Orco orthologue has been identified in each studied insect species.
source: However, these data do not explain the presence of three different Orco variants in the firebrat. So far only one Orco orthologue has been identified in each studied insect species (e.g., Krieger et al., 2003; Pitts et al., 2004; Smadja et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: All T. domestica Orco variants were found to be expressed in antennae, suggesting their involvement in chemosensation.
source: All T. domestica variants were found to be expressed in antennae, suggesting their involvement in chemosensation.
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR data and inferred from the expression pattern.

claim: TdomOrco3 has an amino acid exchange of a functional important residue from asparagine to glutamic acid at position 466.
source: TdomOrco3 even has an amino acid exchange of a functional important residue from asparagine to glutamic acid at position 466.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Residue D466 was demonstrated as critical for the ion channel function in D. melanogaster.
source: This residue was demonstrated as critical for the ion channel function in D. melanogaster, where substitution of D466 with amino acids other than glutamic acid resulted in a substantial reduction in channel activity, but substitution to glutamic acid leads to an increase in sensitivity of the heteromeric receptor complex (Kumar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2013.

claim: Substitution of D466 with amino acids other than glutamic acid resulted in a substantial reduction in channel activity.
source: This residue was demonstrated as critical for the ion channel function in D. melanogaster, where substitution of D466 with amino acids other than glutamic acid resulted in a substantial reduction in channel activity, but substitution to glutamic acid leads to an increase in sensitivity of the heteromeric receptor complex (Kumar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2013.

claim: Substitution of D466 to glutamic acid leads to an increase in sensitivity of the heteromeric receptor complex.
source: This residue was demonstrated as critical for the ion channel function in D. melanogaster, where substitution of D466 with amino acids other than glutamic acid resulted in a substantial reduction in channel activity, but substitution to glutamic acid leads to an increase in sensitivity of the heteromeric receptor complex (Kumar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2013.

claim: Residue D466 is highly conserved across insects including two of the three T. domestica Orcos.
source: Additionally, this residue is highly conserved across insects (Kumar et al., 2013) including two of the three T. domestica Orcos (this study).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and supported by citation.

claim: The antennal expression of T. domestica Orco candidates argues for a potential involvement in chemosensation.
source: While the antennal expression argues for a potential involvement in chemosensation, the existence of three Orco types remains mysterious.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data.

claim: The existence of three Orco types in T. domestica remains mysterious.
source: While the antennal expression argues for a potential involvement in chemosensation, the existence of three Orco types remains mysterious.
evidence: This acknowledges an unexplained finding.

claim: ORs evolved in insects after the emergence of Archaeognatha and Zygentoma.
source: Altogether our data suggests that ORs evolved in insects after the emergence of Archaeognatha and Zygentoma, and therefore long after insects transitioned to a terrestrial lifestyle.
evidence: This is the main evolutionary conclusion based on the comparative data.

claim: ORs evolved long after insects transitioned to a terrestrial lifestyle.
source: Altogether our data suggests that ORs evolved in insects after the emergence of Archaeognatha and Zygentoma, and therefore long after insects transitioned to a terrestrial lifestyle.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of ORs.

claim: At the time when flying insects occurred, the vegetation on earth was rapidly spreading and diversifying.
source: At the time when flying insects occurred, the vegetation on earth was rapidly spreading and diversifying.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of plant evolution.

claim: ORs might not only increase the diversity of detected chemicals, but also allow the olfactory system to rapidly assess airborne odors.
source: ORs might not only increase the diversity of detected chemicals, but also allow the olfactory system to rapidly assess airborne odors.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional advantages of ORs.

claim: Fast response time is especially important for insects for which stimulus contact is very short.
source: This is especially important for insects for which stimulus contact is very short and a fast response time is critical (Getahun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Getahun et al., 2012.

claim: The oldest flying insect orders Odonta (dragonflies and damselflies) and Ephemeroptera (mayflies) were traditionally considered to be anosmic.
source: The oldest flying insect orders Odonta (dragonflies and damselflies) and Ephemeroptera (mayflies) were traditionally considered to be anosmic, lacking both a glomerular antennal lobe and mushroom body calyces (Strausfeld et al., 1998; Farris, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Strausfeld et al., 1998 and Farris, 2005.

claim: Recent studies have shown that at least dragonflies have an aerial sense of smell.
source: Recent studies have shown that at least dragonflies have an aerial sense of smell (Rebora et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rebora et al., 2012.

claim: The small antennae and the low number of olfactory sensilla in dragonflies will make it challenging to identify putative ORs and Orco in antennal transcriptomes.
source: However the small antennae and the low number of olfactory sensilla will make it even more challenging to identify putative ORs and Orco in antennal transcriptomes.
evidence: This is speculation about technical challenges.

claim: ORs were definitely present in the last common ancestor of 'hemi'- and holometabolan insects at least 318–300 million years ago.
source: ORs were definitely present in the last common ancestor of 'hemi'- and holometabolan insects at least 318–300 million years ago, with Orco present in both groups (this study, Krieger et al., 2003; Pitts et al., 2004; Smadja et al., 2009; Yang et al. 2012).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic distribution of ORs and supported by citations.

claim: Orco was present in both 'hemi'- and holometabolan insects.
source: ORs were definitely present in the last common ancestor of 'hemi'- and holometabolan insects at least 318–300 million years ago, with Orco present in both groups (this study, Krieger et al., 2003; Pitts et al., 2004; Smadja et al., 2009; Yang et al. 2012).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic distribution and supported by citations.

claim: The increasing dispersion of vascular plants together with the development of wings and a secondary wing articulation opened new and wider ranges of habitats and ecological niches for insects and the receptors to find them.
source: The increasing dispersion of vascular plants together with the development of wings and a secondary wing articulation opened new and wider ranges of habitats and ecological niches for insects and the receptors to find them.
evidence: This is speculation about the ecological context of OR evolution.

claim: Orco evolved after the bristletails split from its last common ancestor with the remaining insects.
source: Our data suggests the evolution of the coreceptor Orco after the bristletails split from its last common ancestor with the remaining insects.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and inferred from the comparative data.

claim: An olfactory system that relies both on ORs and Orco seems to have evolved after the emergence of wings.
source: However, an olfactory system that relies both on ORs and Orco seems to have evolved after the emergence of wings.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and inferred from the comparative data.
